say: Welcome, Number Sleuths! Every number hides clues in its digits. Today we use the clues to find mystery numbers, build the biggest and the smallest, and prove that we have found every number.
Draw a Th H T O mat. I will call out four digits, one at a time. Write each digit in a box straight away. No moving!
Who made the biggest number? Where did you put the 9? Why there?
With the cards 2, 4, 6 and 8, how many 4-digit numbers between 4000 and 6000 can you make? Write a guess first.
stuck: Stuck: “Which card must go in the thousands place if the number is between 4000 and 6000?”
Missing some: “Keep the 4 in front. Now change the hundreds digit in order: 2, then 6, then 8.”

Ready for more: the Go further what-if on the slide (cards 2, 4, 5, 8: 12 numbers between 4000 and 6000). Or: “How many numbers can you make altogether with the four cards?” (24: six start with each card.)

say: “Greatest number from 4, 0, 8, 1. The thousands place is worth the most, so the biggest digit goes there: 8. Then 4, then 1, then 0: 8410.”
“Smallest. I want the smallest digit first, but 0 cannot go first or it is not a 4-digit number. So 1 goes first, then 0, then 4, then 8: 1048.”
“Greatest odd number from 2, 9, 6, 0. An odd number ends in an odd digit. The only odd card is 9, so I put 9 in the ones place FIRST. Then the biggest of the rest, in order: 6, 2, 0. So 6209.”
“3-digit numbers from 0, 3, 6. I fix the first digit: 3. Then 306, 360. Next first digit: 6. Then 603, 630. 0 cannot go first. So there are 4 numbers, and my list shows I have them all.”

do: Ask: “Which place is worth the most?”
Ask: “Where does the odd digit of an odd number go?”
Ask: “How do you know your list has every number?”
stuck: Hint 2: “For odd or even, decide the ones digit first.”
Hint 3: “Make a list: fix the first digit, then go in order from smallest.”

say: “How do you know you found ALL the numbers in your list?”
ask: No. 0357 is really 357, a 3-digit number, so the smallest 4-digit number is 3057. We know a list is complete because we fixed the first digit and listed the rest in order from smallest, so nothing is missed or repeated.

say: “Sleuths use every clue and check every case. Today you made lists in order and proved you had them all.”

p3l1-title.note: Objective: Read and build 4-digit numbers by place value; make the greatest, smallest, odd, even and closest numbers from digit cards; list every number in order (heuristic: make a list in order); solve clue puzzles and continue number patterns (heuristic: look for a pattern). Materials: Digit cards 0–9 (two sets per child), a place value mat (Th H T O), mini whiteboards, a 10-sided die or a bag of digit cards 0–9 for the warm-up game. Online: Children cut out the digit cards at the back of the workbook (or write 0–9 on small paper squares) and draw a Th H T O mat on paper. The tutor draws the digits on camera. Time plan (90 minutes, with a named 3-minute float inside talk time): opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 5 (own paper, nobody marked, one show-me for both), warm-up game 5 to 8 (two rounds) and three quick questions 8 to 11, explore 11 to 24 (a Go further what-if is on the explore slide from the start; pairs go to pre-assigned breakout rooms), teaching 24 to 35 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 35 to 40, worksheet 40 to 71 (page 1 in pairs, short teaching, page 2 on their own, a 60-second self-check slide after each page; after question 3 of page 1 any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation; from minute 68 everyone chooses), talk time 71 to 79 (volunteers first, pass is fine), exit ticket 79 to 85, look back 85 to 88, stamp and close 88 to 90. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child; the tutor never announces who is on which page and invites the whole group, never one child. If the class is behind, children finish the last question of each page at home; the check slides cover it.

p3l1-warmcheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 5. Sneak-peek puzzles: two small puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Give about 1 minute for each puzzle, then say "show me" ONCE for both: children hold up their paper with both answers in one camera hold-up (about 30 seconds). SAY: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome and so is I do not know. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an ACCESS puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Children write both answers on their own paper and show them only to the tutor on camera (or everybody holds paper to the camera at the same moment, once for both puzzles). No private messages. Never answers read out, never "who got it?". Do not show the answers on the slide now. Puzzle 1 answer (tutor only): 940. Listen for: Biggest digit first, then the next biggest: 9, 4, 0. Puzzle 2 answer (tutor only): 3049. Listen for: Odd means the ones digit is 9 or 3. 0 cannot go first. Try 3049 and 4093: 3049 is smaller. Come back to puzzle 2 at talk time: "Now we know the idea, how could it help?" (volunteers only). Invite the WHOLE group once, never one child; this is an invitation, not a ranking, and any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation after question 3 of page 1. Never announce who is on which page, and never split pairs unless both children agree.

p3l1-warm1.note: Minutes 5 to 8. Biggest number wins. Children draw a Th H T O board on their whiteboard. Draw a digit card (or roll a 10-sided die) four times; after each digit children must write it in one box straight away and cannot move it. Biggest number scores a point. Play TWO rounds: round 1 the biggest number wins, round 2 the SMALLEST number wins (0 cannot go in the thousands box). No third round. The sample round shows the idea: click to show the best possible numbers for 6, 2, 9, 4 (9642 biggest, 2469 smallest). Ask after each round: "Where did you put the 9? Why?" (the thousands place is worth the most). "You got a 1 first. Where should it go when we want the biggest number?" (the ones place: it is small). Listen for the words thousands, hundreds, tens, ones.

p3l1-warm2.note: Minutes 8 to 11. Read each aloud, give thinking time, whiteboards up together, then click to show. Answers: 700; 3045 (watch for 345: there are no hundreds, so we write 0 in the hundreds place); 5000. Three quick questions only. Questions 4 and 5 (100 less than 6050: 5950; which is greater, 7089 or 7098: 7098) are on the take-home box of the Go further page in the workbook.

p3l1-explore1.note: Minutes 11 to 20. Pairs work with their digit cards (online: their paper cards). Ask them to predict first: "How many numbers do you think there are?" Pairs make every 4-digit number between 4000 and 6000 from 2, 4, 6, 8 (each card once), record each one, then decide which is closest to 5000. Hints: "Which card must go first?" "Keep the 4 in front and change the hundreds digit in order." Ready for more: "How many numbers can you make altogether?" (24). GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of explore, so nobody waits): Cards 2, 4, 5, 8 now: how many numbers between 4000 and 6000? Which is closest to 5000? Answer: 12 numbers: 6 start with 4 and 6 start with 5 (2, 4, 5, 8 each once). Closest to 5000: 4852 (148 away); the nearest above is 5248. Any pair may choose it as soon as their first task is done; do not say who is ready for it. Online: pairs are in pre-assigned breakout rooms (set up before the lesson, auto-move in and auto-close with a timer, about 45 seconds per move). Visit each breakout room at least once while the pairs work (about 1 minute per room).

p3l1-explore2.note: Minutes 20 to 24. Let pairs keep working, then gather them. Answers: 1) 6 numbers: 4268, 4286, 4628, 4682, 4826, 4862. 2) Every number must start with 4 (2 is too small, 6 and 8 are too big). Then list in order: hundreds digit 2 (4268, 4286), 6 (4628, 4682), 8 (4826, 4862). Two each, so 6. 3) 4862, only 138 below 5000. Above 5000 the smallest we can make is 6248, which is 1248 away. Praise pairs who listed in order: that is today's first heuristic, make a list in order.

p3l1-teach1.note: Teach. Children lay out 4, 0, 8, 1 on their mats. Think-aloud: "Greatest number from 4, 0, 8, 1. The thousands place is worth the most, so the biggest digit goes there: 8. Then 4, then 1, then 0: 8410. Smallest: I want the smallest digit first, but 0 cannot go first or it is not a 4-digit number. So 1 goes first, then 0, then 4, then 8: 1048." Ask: "Is 0148 a 4-digit number?" (No, it is 148.)

p3l1-we1.note: Click through the steps. Think-aloud: "Odd numbers end in an odd digit. The only odd card is 9, so I put 9 in the ones place FIRST. Then I make the rest as big as I can: 6, 2, 0. So 6209." Ask before step 3: "Smallest number is 2069. Why is that not the answer?" (it ends in 9, so it is odd). Common error: making 9620 first and then trying to fix it.

p3l1-we2.note: Click through. Draw a quick number line from 3000 to 5000 with 4000 in the middle and mark 3741 and 4137 on it. Think-aloud: "The closest number is either just above or just below 4000, so I make both and compare." To find how far 3741 is from 4000, count on: 3741 → 3800 is 59, 3800 → 4000 is 200, so 259.

p3l1-try1.note: Whiteboards. a) 6510. b) 1056 (1 first, then 0). c) The odd cards are 1 and 5. Ending in 1: 6501. Ending in 5: 6105. 6501 is greater. Ask: "How did you decide which odd card goes last?" (try both and compare).

p3l1-teach2.note: Teach the heuristic MAKE A LIST IN ORDER. Click to add each row. Think-aloud: "I fix the first digit: 3. The other cards are 0 and 6, smallest first: 306, then 360. Next first digit: 6: 603, 630. 0 cannot go first. 4 numbers, and the list shows I have them all." Your turn (whiteboards): 5, 5, 2 gives 255, 525, 552, only 3, because the two 5s are the same. If time: 1, 2, 3 gives 6 numbers (123, 132, 213, 231, 312, 321).

p3l1-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Putting 0 first for the smallest number (0357 is really 357, a 3-digit number). (2) For the greatest odd number, making the greatest number first and then trying to fix it, instead of choosing the ones digit first. (3) Listing numbers in a random order, so some are missed or written twice (especially with the two 5s in Q2).

p3l1-break.note: Five minutes. Try 3021 (3 jumps, 0 claps, 2 knee taps, 1 toe touch), then 1203 and 2110. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

p3l1-teachpat.note: Teach the heuristic LOOK FOR A PATTERN before worksheet page 1 (Q3). Ask first: "What comes next?" Some children say 4930 (take away 10 each time) because they only checked the first jump. Click to show each jump. Then: "Some patterns add the same amount every time, some grow. Write the jumps between the numbers to find out."

p3l1-ws1.note: Minutes 42 to 55. Walk around. Ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. For Q1d check that pairs try a number above AND below 5000. For Q2 check that they fix the first digit and go in order, and that they do not write 2505 twice. PAGE 1 CLOCK (42 to 55): about 2 minutes to hand out and get started, then pairs auto-move to their pre-assigned breakout rooms (about 45 seconds), about 9.5 minutes of pair work with the room timer on, and auto-close back to the main room (about 45 seconds). Visit each room once. Items not finished are finished at home; the check slide covers them.

p3l1-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1c: the odd cards are 3, 5 and 7; ending in 3 gives 7503, ending in 5 gives 7305, ending in 7 gives 5307. Q2: 3 numbers start with 2 and 6 start with 5 (the two 5s are the same, so 5 numbers are not doubled). Q3a take away 100; b add 1111; c the jumps are 1, 2, 3, 4, so next 5 and 6; d keep adding 250: 4000, 4250, 4500, 4750, 5000 (yes, it is in the pattern), then 5250 right after it. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and hold the corrected page up to the camera once. Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l1-teachrename.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4). Show it with place value blocks or a drawing if possible: 10 hundreds make 1 thousand. Common error: writing the parts side by side, 3 | 12 | 5 | 14, to get 312514. Ask: "Can a place hold more than 9?" (Not when we write the number: we must rename.)

p3l1-teachclues.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). Use ONE clue at a time and fill one box at a time. Each clue takes two clicks: first the step appears, then its digit appears in the chart. Finish by checking every clue against 2356 aloud. Ask: "Which clue did you use first? Why that one?" (Clue 1 gives a digit straight away.)

p3l1-ws2.note: Page 2, on your own: Q4 place value puzzles; Q5(a) what number am I?; then Q5(b) and Q6 (digits that add up to 3) if you have time. Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson. For Q5b ask: "Which four different digits can add up to only 6?"

p3l1-ws2ans.note: Click each answer after a child explains. Q4b: 7305 = 6000 + 1300 + 5. Q5a: thousands 6, ones half of 6 = 3, hundreds = 6 + tens + 3; a digit is at most 9, so tens is 0 and hundreds is 9. Q5b: the smallest four different digits, 0 + 1 + 2 + 3, already add up to 6, so the digits must be 0, 1, 2, 3. Odd means it ends in 1 or 3. Q6b: the counts 1, 3, 6 go up by 2, then 3. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and hold the corrected page up to the camera once. Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l1-stretch.note: Answers: 1) 1027 (start 1, then 0; the last two digits must add to 9 and cannot be 0 or 1, so 2 then 7). 2) 20 (ten times in the ones place: 5, 15, …, 95; ten times in the tens place: 50 to 59; 55 has two 5s). 3) 63, 127 (double and add 1; or the jumps double: 2, 4, 8, 16, then 32 and 64).

p3l1-challenge.note: SUPPORT FOR THE CORE (if time) ITEMS, only for children who choose them. Q5(b): three different digits that add up to 4 are 0, 1, 3 (smallest 103, greatest 310); in Q5(b) FOUR different digits add up to 6, and 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 is the smallest possible sum, so the digits must be 0, 1, 2, 3. Q6: fix the first digit and list in order, as in the 3-digit case (digits that add up to 3: 3 gives 300; 2 gives 210, 201; 1 gives 120, 111, 102; 6 numbers, with counts 1, 2, 3). Do not tell them the 4-digit answer. GO FURTHER: pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) Greatest 9810 (9 = 8 + 1 + 0). Smallest 3012 (the smallest sum of three different digits is 0 + 1 + 2 = 3). 2) 2341 (6 numbers start with 1; then 2134, 2143, 2314, 2341).

p3l1-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? What do we know? Where should we start? For Q1: "To make the number greatest, what should the thousands digit be?" For Q2: "Can you list the numbers that start with 1 in order?"

p3l1-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: the big idea is to decide the most important place first. For the smallest, ask: "Could the thousands digit be 1 or 2?" (No: three DIFFERENT digits add up to at least 0 + 1 + 2 = 3.) Q2: some children notice that 6 numbers start with each card, so the 7th to 12th numbers start with 2; then they only need to list those in order.

p3l1-talk.note: Minutes 71 to 79. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: No. 0357 is really 357, a 3-digit number. The smallest 4-digit number is 3057: the smallest digit that is not 0 goes first, then 0. Follow-up: "How do you know you found ALL the numbers in a list?" (We fixed the first digit and listed the rest in order, so nothing is missed or repeated.) Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME FLOAT: this part holds the lesson's named 3-minute float. If you are behind, shorten talk time (one discussion question, then the partner share); if you are on time, use the full time for the second question and the return to sneak-peek puzzle 2. Never take time from the exit ticket, look back or stamp. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a pass is always fine and so is sharing with a partner. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and nobody is told they were wrong in front of the group. Nobody is called on by name.

p3l1-exit.note: Minutes 79 to 85. Answer: smallest 3068; greatest odd 8603 (3 is the only odd card, so it goes in the ones place). Extension: with the cards 1, 2, 3, 4, how many 4-digit numbers can you make? How many are odd? (24 numbers; 12 are odd.) Answers are shown only to the tutor on camera (own paper). Never mark or read out answers in front of the group. Reflection (look back) follows on the next slide: allow 3 minutes, 2 for the children plus a short share.

p3l1-reflect.note: Minutes 85 to 88. Look back: short and safe. SAY: "Turn to the last page of today and find Look back. Tick or write one thing for each line. There are no right answers, and you may pass on any line." Give the children a full 2 minutes, then a short share (the slide has 3 minutes). The page is never collected, marked or read out in front of the group. Children keep their page. The tutor does not see the page, so say: "If something is still puzzling you, you can show this page to a grown-up at home, or tell me at the start of next lesson." At the start of the next lesson, in the open session, invite anyone who would like another look at a puzzle (volunteers only, by hand signal or in the chat; never a private message). Invite volunteers only (one or two) to share something they did well, or what helped. Praise the strategy ("you drew it and that got you unstuck"), not the speed or the answer. Then stamp the journal and close (minutes 88 to 90).
